chem-chemical-reactions-basics: A chemical reaction rearranges atoms — bonds break and re-form, and the molecules change into something new. Rust isn't dirt on iron; it's iron atoms bonding with oxygen. When you burn wood, cook an egg, or digest food, you're running chemical reactions. The atoms themselves are never created or destroyed — they just change partners.
chem-reactants-products: Every reaction starts with reactants and ends with products: the starting molecules on the left of the arrow, the new molecules on the right. Wood plus oxygen (reactants) becomes ash, smoke, and heat (products). Reading a reaction equation is like reading a recipe — same atoms in, different combinations out, with nothing lost or gained along the way.
chem-conservation-of-mass: In any chemical reaction, mass is conserved: the total weight of the products exactly equals the total weight of the reactants. Burn a log and the ash plus smoke plus gases weigh precisely what the log plus oxygen did — nothing is destroyed, only rearranged. Lavoisier proved this with sealed-glass experiments in the 1770s, turning chemistry into a quantitative science.
chem-lavoisier-revolution: Antoine Lavoisier gave chemistry its modern bones: he named oxygen and hydrogen, showed that burning and breathing are the same kind of reaction, and proved mass is conserved by weighing everything in sealed vessels. His balance-based methods replaced alchemy's guesswork. The French Revolution cut his career short — he was guillotined in 1794.
chem-exothermic-reactions: Exothermic reactions release energy — usually as heat and light. Burning wood, rusting iron, and digesting food are all exothermic; even a hand warmer's iron powder rusts faster on purpose to give off heat. The energy comes from new bonds being stronger than the old ones. Fireworks, engines, and your own metabolism all run on exothermic chemistry.
chem-endothermic-reactions: Endothermic reactions absorb energy from their surroundings, which is why they feel cold. Dissolve ammonium nitrate in water and the beaker frosts over — the same chemistry inside instant cold packs. Cooking eggs and photosynthesis are endothermic too: they take energy in to build new bonds. The equation tells the story: energy on the left side of the arrow means the reaction needs it.
chem-activation-energy: Most reactions need a push before they'll start — the activation energy, like a boulder needing a shove before it can roll downhill. A match's heat supplies the push for burning paper; once started, the reaction releases more energy than the shove cost. That's why gasoline sits calmly in a can but explodes when sparked, and why food needs cooking to start its chemistry.
chem-catalysts: A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up — it lowers the activation energy, letting molecules react faster, then emerges unchanged to do it again. Your body runs on catalysts called enzymes; cars use catalytic converters; industry uses catalysts to make everything from fertilizer to plastic. A single catalyst molecule can enable millions of reactions before retiring.
chem-catalytic-converter: The catalytic converter under your car is a chemistry lab in a metal box: a honeycomb coated with platinum, palladium, and rhodium breaks down toxic exhaust gases into harmless ones. Carbon monoxide becomes carbon dioxide, and nitrogen oxides become nitrogen gas. It works because the hot exhaust energy plus the metal catalysts push the reactions to completion in milliseconds.
chem-oxidation-reduction: Oxidation and reduction are a matched pair — when one atom loses electrons (oxidation), another gains them (reduction). Rust is iron being oxidized; the flame that burns fuel is rapid oxidation; batteries run on the electron flow between the two halves. The old name for oxidation was burning, but the same electron shuffle powers digestion, bleach, and every rechargeable device.
chem-combustion-reaction: Combustion is burning: a fuel reacts rapidly with oxygen, releasing heat and light. The classic fuel is a hydrocarbon — wood, gas, candle wax — and the products are carbon dioxide and water. It's the same reaction whether it's a campfire, a car engine, or a candle, just at different speeds. Your body 'burns' food with the same chemistry, minus the flame.
chem-fire-triangle: Fire needs three things at once: fuel, oxygen, and heat — the fire triangle. Remove any one and the fire dies: water cools the heat, foam smothers the oxygen, and clearing brush removes fuel. Firefighters and extinguisher design are all about breaking the triangle. Even the smallest flame is a chain reaction that keeps the triangle intact.
chem-rusting: Rust is iron slowly burning — iron atoms reacting with oxygen and water to form iron oxide, a flaky brown compound that's weaker than the original metal. It's a slow, cold fire that eats through bridges, ships, and car bodies over years. Unlike combustion, rusting releases heat too slowly to ignite, but it's the same oxidation chemistry, just going at a crawl.
chem-tarnishing: Tarnishing is a metal's surface reacting with the air — silver darkens as it reacts with sulfur compounds, copper turns green as it forms patina, and even gold can dull slightly. It's oxidation at the surface only, a thin film of corrosion rather than deep decay. A polish removes the tarnish layer, which is why silverware brightens with a rub: you're wiping away the reacted skin.
